mentioned in issue #19369

The example files here are good examples of SFTP fragmentation, but to test SSH segmentation into multiple TCP segments, you want to ensure that TCP TSO is turned off (or the MTU smaller if you're capturing on a loopback interface.)

Yeah, sorry I’m not sure about how to do that. Capture is done between Virtualbox Ubuntu instances. I see the MTU that I set, but packet are larger than this setting. Can you guide me here?

Also it looks like TCP reassembly cannot handle duplicate packets. Is this a fact, or am I doing something wrong?

Cheers.

https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/linux-on-z?topic=offload-tcp-segmentation is a fairly good guide to enabling and disabling some of the segmentation offload features (https://docs.kernel.org/networking/segmentation-offloads.html) in the kernel.

You want to disable `gro` on a receiver and `gso` on a sender (possibly also `tso` and `sg` on a sender as well), or otherwise the kernel will help you out by combining certain packets together (before they reach the point of capture) so that they're larger than what's actually on the network.

TCP reassembly does handle duplicate packets, in the sense of packets that reuse TCP segment numbers (or are overlapping.) It should handle that even when the out of order processing is off (it is off by default because it can cause a TCP stream to completely stop being processed by waiting for a segment not in the capture that will never come.) So it handles duplicate packets that are resent by the TCP layer.

TCP reassembly doesn't handle protocols that don't simply use TCP's reliability but resend packets themselves while using new TCP sequence numbers. Such protocols would need their own fragment numbers. SSH doesn't do that. For one thing, it would make decryption impossible.

Can you separate out the SFTP changes and submit them in a separate MR? We can probably get that in without having to worry about the other changes; this current MR is trying to do several different things at once.
mentioned in merge request !12463

The recipient channel is not necessarily the client channel number. It is possible (primarily with remote port forwarding) for the MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN to come from the server and the MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN_CONFIRMATION from the client, in which case the recipient channel would be the server.

According to the RFC, it is possible for channels to be closed and then the same channel number to be reused (not necessarily paired with the same channel number on the other side.) I'm not sure how common that is, but it wouldn't be handled by this.
